questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of India was established in:

options.option_text: 1 January 1949 (post-nationalisation)
1 April 1935 — based on Hilton Young Commission recommendations
26 January 1950
15 August 1947

questions.explanation: RBI established 1 April 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 — based on the Hilton Young Commission (Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, 1926). Headquartered initially in Calcutta; moved to Bombay (Mumbai) in 1937. Started as a private shareholder bank; nationalised on 1 January 1949 under the Reserve Bank (Transfer of Public Ownership) Act, 1948. First Indian Governor — C.D. Deshmukh (1943-49). Current Governor (since Dec 2024) — Sanjay Malhotra.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Reserve Bank of India?

options.option_text: Issuer of currency notes (except ₹1)
Banker to the Government of India and state governments (most)
Direct lender to industries and individuals
Lender of last resort to commercial banks

questions.explanation: RBI does NOT lend to industries or individuals directly — it's a 'central' bank, not a 'commercial' bank. Real RBI functions: (1) Issue of currency (notes ≥ ₹2; ₹1 notes + coins issued by Govt of India, but RBI distributes); (2) Banker / debt manager to the Centre + most states (J&K and Sikkim used to be exceptions, now also under RBI); (3) Banker's bank — maintains CRR/SLR with itself, lender of last resort; (4) Custodian of forex reserves; (5) Monetary policy + regulation of banks; (6) Promotional roles (DICGC, NABARD set-up).

questions.stem: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of RBI, set up by the 2016 amendment to RBI Act, has how many members?

options.option_text: 4 (all RBI)
6 — 3 from RBI + 3 external (appointed by Govt)

questions.explanation: MPC — 6 members. From RBI: Governor (chairperson), Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one officer of RBI nominated by Central Board. External: 3 economists/bankers appointed by Central Government for 4-year non-renewable terms. Decisions by majority vote; in case of tie, Governor has the casting vote. Mandate: maintain CPI inflation at 4% ±2% (revised by Govt every 5 years). MPC sets the REPO RATE — RBI's main policy rate. Meets at least 6 times a year.

questions.stem: The 'Repo Rate' is the rate at which:

options.option_text: Commercial banks lend to RBI
RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities (sale-and-repurchase)
Banks lend among themselves overnight
RBI buys forex from the market

questions.explanation: Repo (repurchase agreement) — bank sells G-secs to RBI today and repurchases at a higher price tomorrow; the difference = interest = repo rate. REVERSE repo — opposite direction (RBI borrows from banks). Other RBI rates: MSF (Marginal Standing Facility, repo + 0.25%), Bank Rate (= MSF normally), CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio), SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio). When RBI hikes repo → cost of funds for banks rises → lending rates rise → demand cools → inflation falls (textbook effect).

questions.stem: The 'Cash Reserve Ratio' (CRR) is the minimum fraction of:

options.option_text: A bank's net worth that must be retained as gold
A bank's NDTL (Net Demand and Time Liabilities) that must be kept with RBI in cash, earning no interest
Bank capital lent to government
Money parked in mutual funds

questions.explanation: CRR — kept as cash with RBI (no interest paid). Stipulated under Section 42 of RBI Act, 1934. Currently 4% (subject to MPC revisions). Distinct from SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio, ~18%) — kept in cash, gold, or government securities WITH THE BANK ITSELF, not with RBI; SLR earns interest. Higher CRR → less money for banks to lend → cools credit growth. CRR was once as high as 15% in early 1990s; gradually reduced as part of liberalisation.

questions.stem: Currency notes of denomination ₹1 are issued by:

options.option_text: Reserve Bank of India
The Government of India (Ministry of Finance) — signed by the Finance Secretary
State Bank of India
SEBI

questions.explanation: ₹1 notes — issued by Government of India under the Coinage Act, 2011 (signed by Finance Secretary). All other notes (₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500, ₹2000) issued by RBI under RBI Act, 1934 — signed by the Governor. Coins (all denominations) are minted by Govt of India at four India Government Mints (Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Noida). RBI just distributes ₹1 notes and all coins through its branches.

questions.stem: RBI follows the 'Minimum Reserve System' to issue currency. Under this system, the minimum reserve required to be maintained is:

options.option_text: ₹100 crore — of which ₹85 crore in foreign securities, ₹115 crore in gold
₹200 crore — ₹115 crore in gold + ₹85 crore in foreign securities
Equivalent to 25% of currency in circulation
No minimum reserve required

questions.explanation: Minimum Reserve System — adopted from 1956 (replacing Proportional Reserve System). RBI maintains minimum reserves of ₹200 crore at all times — ₹115 crore in gold and ₹85 crore in foreign securities. Above this floor, RBI can issue any amount of currency. Earlier Proportional system required ≥40% of notes-in-circulation backed by gold + sterling — became impractical post-WW2.

questions.stem: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requires scheduled commercial banks to maintain a portion of their Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) in which prescribed liquid assets?

options.option_text: Cash deposited with RBI, government bonds, and foreign currency reserves
Cash in hand, gold, and unencumbered approved government securities
Treasury bills, commercial papers, and inter-bank term deposits
Cash with RBI, fixed deposits, and approved debentures of public sector units

questions.explanation: B is correct because SLR must be maintained in cash in hand, gold, and unencumbered approved securities (primarily government securities). Cash deposited with RBI counts toward CRR, not SLR — a very common confusion. Commercial papers and inter-bank deposits are not classified as approved SLR-eligible liquid assets under RBI guidelines.

questions.stem: Which RBI instrument is specifically designed to bridge the Central Government's temporary mismatch between receipts and expenditures within a financial year?

options.option_text: Treasury Bills issued in the open market to address revenue shortfalls
Ways and Means Advances (WMA) extended directly to the Government
Market Stabilisation Scheme bonds floated to bridge the fiscal gap
Overdraft facilities channelled through nationalised public sector banks

questions.explanation: B is correct because Ways and Means Advances (WMA) are short-term credit lines RBI extends to the Central and State Governments to bridge intra-year cash-flow gaps, repayable within 90 days. Treasury Bills are a market borrowing tool, not an RBI-direct bridge. MSS bonds are used to sterilise excess systemic liquidity, not to fund government expenditure shortfalls.

questions.stem: How does the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) fundamentally differ from the standard overnight repo under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF)?

options.option_text: MSF allows banks to borrow at a rate lower than the policy repo rate
Banks may pledge SLR-eligible securities beyond the mandatory SLR buffer under MSF
MSF transactions are settled on a fortnightly basis unlike daily repo auctions
MSF is accessible exclusively to foreign banks operating in India

questions.explanation: B is correct because MSF uniquely permits banks to borrow overnight from RBI by dipping into their mandatory SLR holdings (up to 2% of NDTL), which standard repo does not allow. The MSF rate is 25 basis points above the repo rate (a penal premium), making Option A factually incorrect. MSF is available to all scheduled commercial banks, not only foreign banks.

questions.stem: As per RBI's Priority Sector Lending (PSL) guidelines, what is the mandated overall PSL target for domestic scheduled commercial banks expressed as a share of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC)?

options.option_text: 35% of ANBC with sub-limits for agriculture and weaker sections
40% of ANBC with sub-limits for agriculture and weaker sections
45% of ANBC with sub-limits for agriculture and weaker sections
50% of ANBC with no separate sub-limits prescribed by RBI

questions.explanation: B is correct: domestic scheduled commercial banks must lend 40% of ANBC to priority sectors, with agriculture at 18% and weaker sections at 12% as mandatory sub-targets. Candidates often confuse 40% (domestic banks) with the 32% target applicable to foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches. The 50% figure with no sub-limits is a fabrication.

questions.stem: The Board for Financial Supervision (BFS), the apex body under RBI that supervises commercial banks, NBFCs, and financial institutions, was constituted in 1994 based on the recommendations of which committee?

options.option_text: Narasimham Committee-I (1991) on Financial Sector Reforms
Narasimham Committee-II (1998) focused on capital adequacy norms
Chakravarty Committee (1985) reviewing monetary policy targets
S. S. Tarapore Committee (1997) on capital account convertibility

questions.explanation: A is correct because Narasimham Committee-I (1991) recommended separating the supervisory function from central banking operations, leading to BFS being set up in November 1994 under RBI's Central Board. Narasimham Committee-II (1998) addressed NPA resolution and capital adequacy — a plausible distractor since both share the same chairman. Chakravarty (1985) dealt with monetary targeting; Tarapore focused on capital account convertibility.

questions.stem: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), operationalised by RBI in April 2022, replaced which instrument as the floor rate of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor?

options.option_text: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate, which formed the LAF upper ceiling
Fixed Rate Reverse Repo (FRRR) rate, which was the previous LAF floor
Open Market Operations (OMO) absorption cut-off rate for sterilisation
Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) T-Bill cut-off rate for liquidity drain

questions.explanation: B is correct: prior to April 8, 2022, the fixed rate reverse repo (at which RBI absorbed surplus liquidity by placing collateral with banks) was the LAF floor. SDF replaced it as the floor because SDF is uncollateralised — RBI absorbs excess liquidity without providing government securities to banks, giving RBI greater flexibility. MSF (Option A) is the LAF ceiling, not floor. MSS and OMOs are separate sterilisation tools outside the LAF corridor.

questions.stem: Under RBI's revised Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework, breaches in which specific combination of parameters trigger mandatory supervisory restrictions on a bank?

options.option_text: Capital Adequacy Ratio (CRAR), Net NPA ratio, and Return on Assets (RoA)
Credit-to-GDP ratio, Tier-1 capital buffer, and interbank exposure limits
Loan-to-deposit ratio, provisioning coverage ratio, and liquidity coverage ratio
Gross NPA to total advances, CASA ratio, and priority sector lending shortfall

questions.explanation: A is correct: PCA monitors three risk dimensions — capital (CRAR and CET-1 ratio), asset quality (Net NPA ratio), and profitability (Return on Assets). Each dimension has threshold levels triggering escalating restrictions on dividends, branch expansion, and lending. Credit-to-GDP is a Basel macroprudential buffer indicator, not a PCA trigger. CASA ratio and loan-to-deposit ratio are operational metrics not part of the PCA framework, making Option D a plausible but wrong distractor.
